description: Tasks for finding information you don't know about - assigned when user marks areas as 'unknown'

tasks.title: Find out if they have/had a will
tasks.description: A will determines how assets are distributed and who handles the estate. Finding out if one exists is an important first step.
tasks.why_it_matters: Without a will, state laws determine who inherits (called 'intestate succession'). If there is a will, finding it quickly helps you understand your responsibilities and timeline.
who_to_ask: Other close family members who may have discussed this
Their attorney, if they had one
The bank where they have a safe deposit box
what_to_ask: Do you know if [parent] ever created a will?
Did they ever mention having legal documents prepared?
Do you know if they worked with an estate planning attorney?
Have you seen any documents about what should happen after they're gone?
where_to_look: Home office, filing cabinet, or desk drawers
Safe deposit box at their bank (may need death certificate to access)
With their attorney - check their address book or old checkbook for legal payments
County probate court - some people file wills there for safekeeping
Their email for correspondence with attorneys
tasks.if_none: If they didn't have a will, that's okay. The estate will be distributed according to your state's intestate succession laws. A probate attorney can explain what that means for your family.
tips: Don't panic if you can't find one right away - it may take time
Check for multiple versions - only the most recent valid will matters
An attorney's office may have the original even if they retired
Some states have online will registries

tasks.title: Find out if they have/had a trust
tasks.description: A trust is a legal arrangement that can help assets pass outside of probate. Trusts are less common than wills, but important to know about.
tasks.why_it_matters: If a trust exists, assets in it typically transfer faster and more privately than through probate. The trustee (who may be you) has specific responsibilities.
who_to_ask: Other family members who handled their parents' estates
what_to_ask: Did [parent] ever mention setting up a trust?
Do you know if they did any estate planning beyond a basic will?
Did they ever talk about avoiding probate?
Did an attorney ever mention a 'living trust' or 'revocable trust'?
where_to_look: Same places as a will - home office, safe deposit box
Their attorney's office
Financial institutions - trusts are sometimes set up through banks
Look for documents titled 'Trust Agreement' or 'Declaration of Trust'
tasks.if_none: Most people don't have trusts - they're more common for larger estates or specific planning needs. If there's no trust, the estate goes through normal probate (if needed).
tips: A trust only matters if assets were transferred into it
There may be both a will and a trust - they serve different purposes
The person who set it up is the 'grantor' or 'settlor'

tasks.title: Find out what property they own/owned
tasks.description: Real estate (homes, land, rental properties) is often a significant asset and has specific legal requirements for transfer.
tasks.why_it_matters: Property in the deceased's name alone may need to go through probate. Property owned jointly often passes automatically to the other owner.
who_to_ask: Their accountant or tax preparer (property shows up on tax returns)
Their real estate agent if they bought or sold recently
what_to_ask: Do you know what properties [parent] owned?
Is the house in their name, jointly owned, or in a trust?
Do they own any rental properties, vacation homes, or land?
Did they ever mention owning property you haven't seen?
where_to_look: Property tax bills - these arrive annually and list property addresses
Their most recent tax return (Schedule E for rentals, mortgage interest deductions)
County recorder or assessor websites - search by name to find deeds
Mortgage statements
Homeowner's insurance policies
tasks.if_none: If they rented or didn't own property, that's one less thing to handle. Focus on other assets and accounts.
tips: Check how title is held - 'joint tenancy' or 'tenants by entirety' usually means automatic transfer to survivor
Property in multiple states may require probate in each state
Time-share or vacation club memberships count as property interests

tasks.title: Find out about their financial accounts
tasks.description: Understanding what bank accounts, investment accounts, and retirement accounts exist helps you manage the estate and find all assets.
tasks.why_it_matters: Financial accounts may be the primary source of funds for the estate. Retirement accounts like 401(k)s and IRAs have designated beneficiaries and pass outside probate.
what_to_ask: Do you know what bank they used?
Did they have a financial advisor or brokerage account?
Do you know about any retirement accounts from their job?
Did they ever mention having accounts you don't have access to?
where_to_look: Their mail - statements come monthly or quarterly
Their email for account notifications
Their most recent tax return (1099s list account sources, Schedule B for interest/dividends)
Checkbook or debit card - identifies their bank
Old pay stubs or benefits paperwork for retirement accounts
National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits (for old 401ks)
tasks.if_none: If you can't find accounts, there may still be unclaimed funds. Use your state's unclaimed property database and the National Registry of Unclaimed Retirement Benefits.
tips: Retirement accounts (401k, IRA, pension) pass by beneficiary designation, not will
Joint accounts typically pass to the surviving owner automatically
Check for automatic payments - they reveal active accounts

tasks.title: Find out about life insurance policies
tasks.description: Life insurance can provide immediate funds for expenses and goes directly to beneficiaries without waiting for probate.
tasks.why_it_matters: Life insurance payouts are usually quick (2-4 weeks) and can help cover immediate expenses like funeral costs. The money goes to named beneficiaries, not the estate.
who_to_ask: Their employer's HR department (many jobs include life insurance)
Veterans Affairs if they served in the military
what_to_ask: Do you know if [parent] had life insurance through work or personally?
Did they ever mention having a policy?
Who is their insurance agent or company?
Did they serve in the military? (VA offers life insurance)
where_to_look: Their mail and email for premium notices or policy statements
Their bank statements for automatic premium payments
Their employer's benefits paperwork
Old tax returns - some policies generate 1099s
NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator (free service)
MIB Group (maintains records of life insurance applications)
tasks.if_none: If there's no life insurance, that's common - not everyone has it. Other assets will need to cover final expenses.
tips: Workplace policies often end when employment ends - check if they were retired
Some policies have a 'paid-up' status where no more premiums are due
Credit cards and mortgages sometimes include life insurance
The claim process is usually straightforward once you find the policy
